chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Rib'i ibn Abdillah, from a man, from Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created the Prophets from the clay of Illiyeen — their hearts and their bodies — and He created the hearts of the believers from that same clay, and He made the creation of the bodies of the believers from below that. And He created the disbelievers from the clay of Sijjeen — their hearts and their bodies.

Then He blended between the two clays. Thus, from this, a believer begets a disbeliever and a disbeliever begets a believer, and from here a believer commits a sin and from here a disbeliever does a good deed. So the hearts of the believers yearn toward what they were created from, and the hearts of the disbelievers yearn toward what they were created from.

key_terms.تحن: To yearn/long for — the innate spiritual pull of the heart toward its origin
key_terms.خلط الطينتين: The blending of the two clays — the theological explanation for moral ambiguity in human behavior
key_terms.طينة سجين: The clay of Sijjeen — the substance of the lowest infernal register (83:7), associated with unrighteous souls
key_terms.طينة عليين: The clay of Illiyeen — the substance of the highest celestial register (83:18), associated with righteous souls and the Prophets

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Zayn al-Abidin say about the creation of believers and disbelievers from different clays?
ai.summary: Imam Zayn al-Abidin (peace be upon him) explains the cosmological origin of spiritual disposition: God created the Prophets and the hearts of believers from the noble clay of Illiyeen (the register of the righteous in the highest realm), while the disbelievers were created from the base clay of Sijjeen (the register of the wicked). The blending of these two clays explains why believers sometimes sin and disbelievers sometimes do good, as each naturally inclines toward its original substance. This cosmological framework, rooted in Quranic terminology (83:7, 83:18), provided early Shia audiences with a theological explanation for the diversity of human spiritual states without negating free will.
